summary: The DNA copy number calculator works out DNA copies from the DNA concentration, the template length, number of PCR cycles and the DNA copies after PCR cycle. It is built for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the DNA copy number calculator work?
sections.html:
The DNA copy number calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports DNA copies in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the base weight); then you type in the DNA concentration, the template length, number of PCR cycles and the DNA copies after PCR cycle(s).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in ng/µl.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in base pairs. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as ssDNA (330 Da), ssRNA (340 Da) and dsDNA (660 Da). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in times 10 to the 7. The unit chip switches it to any of the 69 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the DNA copy number calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

DNA copies=602214000000000 × DNA concentration ÷ (base weight × template length)
Initial DNA copies=(2 ^ -number of PCR cycles) × DNA copies after PCR cycle(s)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • DNA, opening in base pairs
  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 7
  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 7
  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 7

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The DNA copy number calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the DNA concentration, the template length and number of PCR cycles — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the DNA copy number calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns DNA copies, derived from the DNA concentration, the template length and number of PCR cycles. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the DNA copy number calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the DNA concentration, the template length, number of PCR cycles and the DNA copies after PCR cycle, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter template length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Template length opens in base pairs and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the DNA copy number calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
